overview: Ancient Mauretania occupied parts of today’s Morocco and Algeria, far north of modern Mauritania. Its towns combined local traditions with Punic and Mediterranean connections. The map ends in 1 BCE, during a kingdom that continued under Juba II and his successors into the first century CE.

periods.title: Mauretanian towns and Mediterranean exchange
periods.summary: Towns such as Volubilis and Lixus had their own institutions, sanctuaries and commercial connections before Roman annexation.

periods.title: A kingdom allied with Rome
periods.summary: Juba II’s dynasty ruled a Roman client kingdom while maintaining royal titles and distinctive public imagery.

periods.title: Annexation after Ptolemy
periods.summary: Rome incorporated the kingdom after the killing of its last king; cities and communities continued under provincial rule.

items.text: At Volubilis, archaeologists uncovered part of an early wall built from unfired bricks on a stone base. Much of the earlier city lies beneath later buildings, so the surviving Roman streets cannot simply be treated as a complete picture of the Mauretanian town.

Punic and Neo-Punic inscriptions from Volubilis attest connections with the Carthaginian world. One inscription names magistrates called suffetes, suggesting that local government borrowed an institutional model without making the city merely a copy of Carthage.

Imported Campanian pottery, transport amphorae and coins from places such as Cadiz show that Volubilis participated in wider exchange. A pot’s place of manufacture helps trace a journey; it does not by itself identify the language or ancestry of its owner.

At Lixus, excavated houses dated to the third or second centuries BCE had two storeys and lacked the central atrium or peristyle familiar from many Roman textbook houses. North African city dwellers had architectural traditions of their own.

Lixus stood on a hill above the Loukkos river, several kilometres from the Atlantic. Its position connected a settlement and its surrounding farmland with river and sea routes, rather than separating city life from the coast.

The sanctuary at Lixus contained several temples built and rebuilt over different periods. Ancient stories associated the place with Hercules and the Garden of the Hesperides, but archaeologists do not treat a mythical origin as an excavation date.

A study of 26 amphora samples from recent Lixus excavations identified several clay fabrics compatible with southern Spain rather than local production. These late Mauretanian and Roman containers show that even a fish-processing centre could import some of its packaging.

A silver coin in the British Museum pairs Juba II’s portrait with Cleopatra Selene’s. The queen appears as a named royal figure in her own right, making a small object evidence for the public presentation of a ruling couple.

Juba II wrote in Greek on geography and other subjects. His works drew on earlier authors and research across a wider Mediterranean world; scholarly activity helped give his court cultural distinction as well as political connections.

A later coin from 11 or 12 CE bears the Latin sample “REX IVBA”, meaning “King Juba”. The use of V for the vowel written u in modern texts is ordinary Latin inscriptional spelling. This surviving coin comes just after the map entry’s 1 BCE endpoint.

On that coin Juba wears a lion skin, while a cornucopia and trident appear on the other side. The museum interprets these as claims about heroic ancestry, prosperity and maritime power: a tiny coin could carry a large royal message.

Roman annexation changed political authority, but Volubilis retained local inhabitants and some earlier institutions. New monuments were added to an existing city. A change of rulers did not mean that its residents woke up without their previous history.

ending.text: The killing of King Ptolemy in 40 CE ended the dynasty, and Roman annexation followed. The map’s 1 BCE endpoint is therefore not the kingdom’s fall. Towns, farming communities and local traditions continued within a changed provincial order.
